title: Facing the Mountain: A True Story of Japanese American Heroes in World War II
author: Daniel James Brown
target_audience: General readers interested in WWII history
Those interested in Japanese American history and experiences
Students and educators studying civil rights and American history
Readers of narrative nonfiction and biography
core_themes: The injustice of Japanese American incarceration
primary_purpose: To chronicle the personal and collective experiences of Japanese American soldiers and their families during World War II, highlighting their courage in battle and at home against profound injustice, and to confront the legacy of prejudice and resilience.

structure_format.organization: Structured around the lives of several Japanese American individuals, weaving together personal histories, military campaigns, and the broader context of internment
features: Maps and archival photos in many editions

key_concepts_lessons: Even in the face of forced incarceration and discrimination, many Japanese Americans chose to serve the country that had wronged them.
Loyalty and patriotism are often complex and deeply personal.
The bravery of the 442nd Regimental Combat Team and the Military Intelligence Service was both an act of courage and a statement against prejudice.
Civil liberties can be fragile, especially in times of war and fear.
The forced relocation and incarceration (internment) of Japanese Americans was a grave injustice with long-lasting repercussions.
notable_features: Focus on individual stories within larger historical events
Highlights both battlefield heroism and domestic struggles against prejudice
Draws on extensive interviews and archival research
Brings fresh perspective to a well-known period of American history
cultural_historical_context: Published in the 2020s as public discussion of historical racism in America gained new urgency, the book re-examines the story of Japanese American soldiers and their families, aligning with an increased interest in underrepresented histories and wartime civil rights abuses.
reception_impact: New York Times bestseller and highly acclaimed for narrative rigor and empathy
Praised for deep research, compelling storytelling, and illuminating a lesser-known side of WWII
Adopted by educators and book clubs to discuss race, citizenship, and American values
Contributed to ongoing conversations about civil liberties, immigration, and identity

They Called Us Enemy by George Takei
